You are implementing one stream of a Python project: repo /Users/yashvi/orange_health_assignemnt (your worktree is a copy of branch feat/demo-build at commit a7b43ed). First run `uv sync --all-extras`.

Read: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-18-demo-scope.md ("Global Constraints", "Review Focus" item 3, **Task 11**), docs/specs/S-C-rule-engine-spec.md §9 (the A1 COMPOSE contract and insight JSON shape), docs/explainer.md §8 and §10 (example messages), and the existing src/aqagent/{types.py,params.py}. `Candidate`, `CandidateKind`, `EventKind`, `Band` (with `.label`) and `StationScore` exist in types.py: use them.

Your task: A1 COMPOSE only. Skip deliver.py, which the orchestrator writes later because it needs the DB.
- src/aqagent/act/facts.py: `ACTION_CATALOGUE` (keyed by (CandidateKind, Band), filtered by persona habits such as "morning run" and the local hour; actions are short imperative phrases like "skip the outdoor run", "keep windows closed", "wear an N95 outside", "open the windows", "go for that run"). `history_facts(history: list[StationScore], at: datetime, tz, episode: dict | None) -> list[str]`, deterministic: "worst since <date>" (highest NowCast in the history before now), "Nth bad morning this week", "back to normal after N hours", "since <local hour>". And `build_insight(candidate: Candidate, *, user: dict, city: str, tz: ZoneInfo, at: datetime, score: StationScore, typical_pm25: float | None, episode: dict | None, history: list[StationScore], absorbed_held: list[Candidate]) -> dict` in the S-C §9 shape. `episode` is a plain dict with opened_at, peak_value, peak_band, peak_at, hours. `user` has name and persona.
- src/aqagent/act/compose.py: `ComposedMessage(body, next_action, generator)`, `template(insight) -> ComposedMessage` (good natural templates per kind × event_kind: spike "jumped sharply", climb "getting worse since …", elevated "stuck above normal for …", floor "has crossed into …", cleared "back to its usual level after …", check_in, released; always one past-context fact and exactly one action; ≤ params.MESSAGE_MAX_CHARS), `validate_message(body, insight) -> list[str]` (length; exactly one action candidate present; every number/date token in the body appears in json.dumps(insight); not a bare "AQI is now N"), `compose(insight, llm, timeout_s=params.LLM_TIMEOUT_S) -> ComposedMessage` (calls the LLM in a thread with a timeout, validates, and falls back to template), and `anthropic_llm(model: str | None = None) -> Callable[[str], str] | None` (None without ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; model default from env AQAGENT_LLM_MODEL or params.DEFAULT_LLM_MODEL). Before writing anthropic_llm, invoke the `claude-api` skill and follow it for the SDK call. The prompt asks for one or two sentences using only the given facts and exactly one of `action_candidates`, returning plain text.
- tests/test_compose.py: every test named in the plan for Task 11, including `test_review_llm_timeout_falls_back`. Tests never call the real API.

Rules: strict TDD (write a test, run it, watch it fail correctly, implement, watch it pass). Don't modify types.py, params.py, clock.py, pyproject.toml or files you don't own. Report needed additions instead. `uv run pytest -q` must be green. Commit on your worktree branch with messages ending in "Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>". Do not push or merge.

Final report (≤250 words): branch, commits, test result, public signatures, three sample template messages, and deviations with what they cost if wrong.

Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: propose it and call this.

The result says which case below applies. When the box shows your question, it ends your turn: write no text after this call, since the recap and question say what the user needs and your work above holds the detail. Otherwise your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, with any question the box did not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead, an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No "@", no leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no "@" anywhere, no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. <system-reminder>
The following MCP servers require authentication before their tools can be used:
plugin:design:figma
plugin:design:intercom
plugin:engineering:asana
plugin:engineering:atlassian
plugin:engineering:datadog

plugin:engineering:linear

Claude cannot start the OAuth flow itself. If the user's request depends on one of these servers (even if they didn't name it explicitly), or they ask about it, tell them that it needs to be authorized — for claude.ai connectors, via their claude.ai connector settings; for other servers, via /mcp — and that the capability is unavailable until they do. Otherwise carry on with the request and do not mention these servers. Do not ask the user for authorization codes, tokens, or callback URLs.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- compound-engineering:ce-adversarial-document-reviewer: Conditional document-review persona for high-stakes documents -- those with significant architectural decisions, new abstractions, or more than 5 requirements. Challenges premises, surfaces unstated assumptions, and stress-tests decisions rather than evaluating document quality. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- compound-engineering:ce-adversarial-reviewer: Conditional code-review persona, selected when the diff is large (>=50 changed lines) or touches high-risk domains like auth, payments, data mutations, or external APIs. Actively constructs failure scenarios to break the implementation rather than checking against known patterns. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write)

- compound-engineering:ce-agent-native-reviewer: Reviews code to ensure agent-native parity -- any action a user can take, an agent can also take. Use after adding UI features, agent tools, or system prompts. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- compound-engineering:ce-ankane-readme-writer: Creates or updates README files following Ankane-style template for Ruby gems. Use when writing gem documentation with imperative voice, concise prose, and standard section ordering. (Tools: All tools)

- compound-engineering:ce-api-contract-reviewer: Conditional code-review persona, selected when the diff touches API routes, request/response types, serialization, versioning, or exported type signatures. Reviews code for breaking contract changes. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write)

- compound-engineering:ce-architecture-strategist: Analyzes code changes from an architectural perspective for pattern compliance and design integrity. Use when reviewing PRs, adding services, or evaluating structural refactors. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- compound-engineering:ce-best-practices-researcher: Researches and synthesizes external best practices, documentation, and examples for any technology or framework. Use when you need industry standards, community conventions, or implementation guidance. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch, mcp__context7__*)

- compound-engineering:ce-code-simplicity-reviewer: Final review pass to ensure code is as simple and minimal as possible. Use after implementation is complete to identify YAGNI violations and simplification opportunities. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- compound-engineering:ce-coherence-reviewer: Reviews planning documents for internal consistency -- contradictions between sections, terminology drift, structural issues, and ambiguity where readers would diverge. Spawned by the document-review skill. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

## 1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai .../artifact/... link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{...}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## 470653a9-ca83-4253-8a6d-0a608e64bb1b
Vercel MCP provides over 200 tools. Capabilities:
Deployments: builds, status/logs/files, aliases, promotions, rollbacks, rolling releases and sharing/access.
Insights: runtime errors/logs, Web Analytics, observability metrics, usage/billing and agent run traces.
Configuration: projects, accounts/teams/access groups, environment variables, domains/pricing/registration, DNS/TLS, routes/redirects, microfrontends, feature flags, Blob stores and Global Config (Edge Config).
Platform: cache artifacts/invalidation, Marketplace integrations, Connect, firewall/protection, KMS, Vercel CI/checks, Sandbox sessions/commands/files/snapshots, drains, webhook inspection and account events.
Collaboration: Toolbar comments, Claude Design imports and documentation search.

Use tool input schemas. Reuse known team/project IDs and connection scope; never guess. Discover only missing scope; ask if the target remains ambiguous.

For failed deployments, inspect state and build logs. For production errors, start with get_runtime_errors, then get_runtime_logs.

Use supported project/deployment/environment/time filters. Follow pagination for complete results; report partial data. Inspect every result. Distinguish observed failures from suspected causes.

Verify changes before reporting completion. Check uncertain writes before retrying. For requires_user_action, return the dashboard URL and leave the action pending.

For access/not-found errors, verify scope and follow reported login/SSO steps.

If MCP fails or lacks an operation, use CLI fallbacks in results, tool descriptions or _meta["vercel.com/cli"]. Follow their mappings and preserve known scope; CLI credentials and defaults are separate.

Never request or print credentials, secrets or private keys. Never decrypt environment values unless requested.

## 9852f30b-ac92-44f4-9234-e65837371ae0
Use this server when the user asks about meetings, notes, transcripts, or calendar information stored in Wispr Flow. For questions that may span multiple connected sources, use the relevant sources needed to answer the request. Read https://notes.wisprflow.ai/shared/ links with resolve_share_link rather than fetching the page. All timestamps returned by these tools are UTC (ISO 8601, ending in 'Z'). Before showing any time to the user, convert it to their local time zone — never present the raw UTC value.

## a71780ce-aa7a-49aa-9524-7672f3ed2c69
Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Before making schema changes, inspect the existing tables so you understand the current structure
- When debugging issues, start by reading the project's logs and its security, performance, and health advisories before making changes
- Look up the project's API URL and its publishable API keys when helping users configure client-side integrations

"""Shared value types. Every layer speaks in these."""
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime
from enum import IntEnum, StrEnum


class Band(IntEnum):
    """US EPA 2024 PM2.5 categories, ordered from best to worst."""

    GOOD = 0
    MODERATE = 1
    USG = 2
    UNHEALTHY = 3
    VERY_UNHEALTHY = 4
    HAZARDOUS = 5

    @property
    def slug(self) -> str:
        return self.name.lower()

    @property
    def is_severe(self) -> bool:
        return self >= Band.VERY_UNHEALTHY

    @property
    def label(self) -> str:
        return {
            Band.GOOD: "good",
            Band.MODERATE: "moderate",
            Band.USG: "unhealthy for sensitive groups",
            Band.UNHEALTHY: "unhealthy",
            Band.VERY_UNHEALTHY: "very unhealthy",
            Band.HAZARDOUS: "hazardous",
        }[self]

    @classmethod
    def parse(cls, value: str | Band) -> Band:
        if isinstance(value, Band):
            return value
        return cls[value.strip().upper()]


class EventKind(StrEnum):
    spike = "spike"
    climb = "climb"
    elevated = "elevated"
    floor = "floor"


EVENT_PRECEDENCE = (EventKind.spike, EventKind.climb, EventKind.elevated, EventKind.floor)


class CandidateKind(StrEnum):
    opened = "opened"
    escalated = "escalated"
    cleared = "cleared"
    check_in = "check_in"
    released = "released"


class Outcome(StrEnum):
    sent = "sent"
    held = "held"
    suppressed = "suppressed"
    no_event = "no_event"


class ReasonCode(StrEnum):
    NO_DATA = "NO_DATA"
    NO_BASELINE = "NO_BASELINE"
    DQ_INVALID = "DQ_INVALID"

    SENT_CLEARED = "SENT_CLEARED"
    SENT_CHECK_IN = "SENT_CHECK_IN"
    SENT_SEVERE_BYPASS = "SENT_SEVERE_BYPASS"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Reading:
    sensor_id: int
    period_end: datetime
    period_start: datetime
    value: float | None
    coverage_pct: float | None = None


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TraceStep:
    layer: str

    def as_dict(self) -> dict:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CheckedReading:
    """S2 output: a reading plus why it was excluded (None = usable). `provisional` = newest hour, glitch check pending."""

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StationScore:

"""Synthetic data builders shared by the tests."""
from __future__ import annotations

import csv
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from functools import lru_cache
from pathlib import Path

from aqagent.types import Reading

UTC = timezone.utc
SAMPLE_CSV = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "samples" / "openaq_pm25_hourly_90d.csv"


def hourly(start: datetime, values, sensor_id: int = 1, coverage: float = 100.0) -> list[Reading]:
    """One Reading per hour starting at `start` (the first period_end). None values are skipped (a gap)."""
    out = []
    for i, v in enumerate(values):
        end = start + timedelta(hours=i)
        if v is None:
            continue
        out.append(Reading(sensor_id, end, end - timedelta(hours=1), float(v), coverage))
    return out


@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def _sample_rows() -> tuple:
    with SAMPLE_CSV.open() as f:
        return tuple(csv.DictReader(f))


def sample_readings(location_id: int) -> list[Reading]:
    out = []
    for r in _sample_rows():
        if int(r["location_id"]) != location_id:
            continue
        end = datetime.fromisoformat(r["period_end_utc"].replace("Z", "+00:00"))
        start = datetime.fromisoformat(r["period_start_utc"].replace("Z", "+00:00"))
        cov = float(r["percent_coverage"]) if r["percent_coverage"] else None
        out.append(Reading(int(r["sensor_id"]), end, start, float(r["value_ugm3"]), cov))
    return sorted(out, key=lambda x: x.period_end)
"""U2 'how harmful': EPA NowCast and the 2024 PM2.5 AQI bands (S-B §2, S-C §4)."""
from __future__ import annotations

import math

from aqagent import params
from aqagent.types import Band

# (upper concentration µg/m³, band, AQI low, AQI high, concentration low), 2024 revision
_BREAKPOINTS = [
    (9.0, Band.GOOD, 0, 50, 0.0),
    (35.4, Band.MODERATE, 51, 100, 9.1),
    (55.4, Band.USG, 101, 150, 35.5),
    (125.4, Band.UNHEALTHY, 151, 200, 55.5),
    (225.4, Band.VERY_UNHEALTHY, 201, 300, 125.5),
    (325.4, Band.HAZARDOUS, 301, 500, 225.5),
]


def _truncate(c: float) -> float:
    return math.floor(c * 10) / 10


def band_for(pm25: float) -> Band:
    c = _truncate(pm25)
    for hi, band, *_ in _BREAKPOINTS:
        if c <= hi:
            return band
    return Band.HAZARDOUS


def aqi_value(pm25: float) -> int:
    c = _truncate(max(pm25, 0.0))
    for hi, _band, i_lo, i_hi, c_lo in _BREAKPOINTS:
        if c <= hi:
            return round((i_hi - i_lo) / (hi - c_lo) * (c - c_lo) + i_lo)
    return 500


def nowcast(window: list[tuple[int, float]]) -> float | None:
    """`window` holds (hours_ago, clean value) pairs. Valid only with 2 of the 3 most recent hours."""
    pts = [(h, c) for h, c in window if 0 <= h < params.NOWCAST_HOURS and c is not None]
    if sum(1 for h, _ in pts if h < 3) < 2:
        return None
    values = [c for _, c in pts]
    hi, lo = max(values), min(values)
    w = 1.0 if hi <= 0 else max(0.5, 1 - (hi - lo) / hi)
    num = sum(w**h * c for h, c in pts)
    den = sum(w**h for h, _ in pts)
    return _truncate(num / den)

## What we're building: Proactive Air Quality Insight Agent

A backend service that watches air quality continuously and decides on its own when, and what, to proactively tell a user. The product goal is "only speak when something is worth knowing", so restraint (not notifying) is as important as detection.

Data source: OpenAQ (https://openaq.org/), 4–5 cities/stations, polled hourly.

### Core requirements (all mandatory)

2. **Insight/trigger logic** — detect patterns, not raw thresholds:

   - sudden spike (sharp jump vs. recent baseline)
   - return to normal after a bad period
   - explicitly handle false positives and missed triggers
   - **primary detection must be a simple learned anomaly/change-point model on recent history** (e.g. rolling z-score / EWMA residuals, CUSUM, Bayesian online change-point) — fixed thresholds alone don't satisfy this.
3. **Dedup / rate limiting** — persistent per-user state of what has already been said; 6 straight bad hours must not produce 6 identical notifications. Re-notify only on a meaningful change.
4. **Message generation** — short natural-language notification text that references relevant past context and includes exactly one clear next action. Not JSON, not a template like "AQI is now 142", not a pure status update.
5. **Per-city / per-user sensitivity** — baselines differ by location: a user in a clean city gets a lower "unusual" bar than one in a naturally dusty region. Sensitivity should derive from each station's own learned baseline, optionally scaled per user.
6. **Observability** — an internal log/endpoint/dashboard showing what fired, when, why, and the exact data that triggered it, so a bad or missing nudge can be debugged later. Suppressed/deduped decisions should be recorded too, not just sent ones.

Out of scope: polished frontend, auth, multi-tenancy. A few hardcoded users per city is fine.

### Bonus

- Decay/cooldown so the system doesn't nag even after a legitimate re-trigger.
- Evaluation harness that replays historical OpenAQ data and reports interesting moments caught vs. missed. Designing ingestion/detection so it can run against a replayed clock (rather than wall-clock "now") makes this nearly free.

### Submission deliverables

GitHub repo, recorded demo video (e.g. Loom), decision/architecture note, transcript of coding tools/AI used, and conversation/notification history. Keep the architecture note and a notification history export in the repo as the work progresses.

## Domain notes

- OpenAQ reports pollutant concentrations (e.g. PM2.5 in µg/m³), not AQI. AQI must be computed from concentrations (e.g. US EPA breakpoints), and the choice should be documented.
- The current OpenAQ API (v3) requires a free API key sent as an `X-API-Key` header; older v1/v2 endpoints are retired. Keep the key in an env var, never in the repo.
- Station readings can be missing, delayed, or duplicated across polls; ingestion should be idempotent and the detector should tolerate gaps.

1	# Air Quality Insight Agent — Demo Scope Implementation Plan
2	
3	> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.
4	
5	**Goal:** Build the demo-scope agent: hourly OpenAQ ingestion for 5 cities, a learned per-station detector, the per-user decision pipeline D1–D8, natural-language notices, a decision log with an explain API, and a replay harness that reports caught vs missed.
6	
7	**Architecture:** A single Python package. Pure functions per layer (S2, U1, U2, D1–D8, A1), wired by a runner that has two triggers: a data run after ingestion, and a clock tick. All state lives in SQL (SQLite locally, Postgres when hosted) through SQLAlchemy Core. Time is always injected. Every evaluation recomputes from the readings known at that moment, so replay equals live.
8	
9	**Tech Stack:** Python 3.13 · uv · SQLAlchemy 2 (Core) · pydantic 2 · httpx · FastAPI + uvicorn · APScheduler 3.x (scheduling and cron parsing) · anthropic SDK (optional) · ruptures (eval extra) · pytest.
10	
11	**Spec:** [docs/explainer.md](../../explainer.md) (design, closed) · [docs/specs/S-C-rule-engine-spec.md](../../specs/S-C-rule-engine-spec.md) (exact logic and parameters) · [docs/specs/S-A-openaq-and-schema.md](../../specs/S-A-openaq-and-schema.md) (API facts, schema) · [docs/requirements.md](../../requirements.md) · [docs/QA.csv](../../QA.csv) (test cases)
12	
13	## Global Constraints
14	
15	- Python `>=3.12` (3.13 locally). Package `aqagent` in `src/aqagent/`. Tests in `tests/`, named `test_<qa id>_<what>` (e.g. `test_qa_ing_10_band_boundaries`), so every test traces to a QA.csv row.
16	- Runtime dependencies are limited to: `sqlalchemy>=2`, `pydantic>=2`, `httpx`, `fastapi`, `uvicorn`, `apscheduler>=3.10,<4`. Optional extras: `llm = ["anthropic"]`, `eval = ["ruptures", "numpy"]`. Dev: `pytest`. Statistics use the standard library only.
17	- Every timestamp is a timezone-aware UTC `datetime`. Local time is derived from `stations.timezone` with `zoneinfo`.
18	- **No code under `src/aqagent/` except `clock.py` may call `datetime.now`, `datetime.utcnow`, `time.time` or `date.today`** (QA-EVAL-05).

27	These are implementation-level clarifications the specs don't settle. They're used by this plan and must be added to the explainer and S-C after the user confirms.
28	
29	1. **Late hours older than a user's last evaluated hour** are scored and stored (so they shape every later window) but don't re-run D2–D8 for that past hour. The decision is written as `no_event · LATE_HOUR_SCORED`. In the common case of a sensor outage, all late hours are newer than the last evaluated hour, so they *are* evaluated in order, as the explainer says.
30	2. **A clock tick writes `NO_DATA`** for a user only when the newest reading is more than 3 h old. Otherwise the tick does only its scheduled work (check-in, release). Every hour still ends up with a decision: either its reading arrives and is evaluated, or the clock records `NO_DATA`.
31	3. **APScheduler** is the cron library: `CronTrigger.from_crontab(expr, timezone=tz)` for check-ins, live and in replay.
32	
33	## Review Focus
34	
35	1. **A late, out-of-order hour** (hour H arrives after H+1..H+3 were evaluated) must not double-count episode transitions or re-send anything. Pinned in Task 10: `test_review_late_hour_does_not_rewind_episode`.
36	2. **DST transitions** in Helsinki and Los Angeles: the repeated or skipped local hour must not crash hour-of-day bucketing, and quiet hours must follow wall-clock time. Pinned in Task 5: `test_review_dst_hour_buckets`.
37	3. **A hanging or slow LLM** must not stall the hourly run: 10 s timeout, then the template fallback. Pinned in Task 11: `test_review_llm_timeout_falls_back`.
38	4. **Overlapping runs** (a slow run still going when the next tick fires) must not double-ingest or double-send. Pinned in Task 14: `test_review_scheduler_no_overlap`.
39	5. **A station or sensor disappears** from OpenAQ (404 or empty results): the run is partial, the sensor goes down the NO_DATA path, and nothing crashes. Pinned in Task 3: `test_review_sensor_404_is_partial`.
40

104	     │ (flap window expires)                                              ▼  │
105	   CLOSED ◄────────────────── 4 consecutive calm hours ────────────── RECOVERING
106	     ▲ │
107	     │ └── trigger within 6 h of close ──► same episode reopens as ACTIVE (flap guard)
108	     │
109	     └──── 24 h of NO_DATA ──► closes quietly: close_reason = 'no_data_timeout', no notice

119	## 7. D3–D8: the per-user pipeline, and the clock
120	
121	### 7.1 Two triggers (FR-CLK-1)
122	
123	- **Data run:** after each ingestion, evaluate every user for every hour that was new or revised.
124	- **Clock tick:** every hour at `:20`, and at each user's check-in time and quiet-hours end, evaluate every user, even with no new data. This is what writes `NO_DATA` decisions, advances the 24 h timeout, releases held notices and runs check-ins.
125	
126	Both write `decisions` rows with `trigger = 'data' | 'clock'`. Every hour ends up with a decision for every user: either its reading arrives and the data run evaluates it, or the clock tick writes `NO_DATA` once the newest reading is more than 3 h old (normal publishing delay isn't silence).
127	
128	**Late hours** older than a user's last evaluated hour are scored and stored, so they shape every later window, but they don't re-run D2–D8 for that past hour: the decision is `no_event · LATE_HOUR_SCORED`. In a sensor outage, all the late hours are newer than the last evaluated one, so they *are* evaluated in order.
129	
130	### 7.2 Layer order
131	
132	The first terminal outcome stops the pipeline. Every layer, including stubs, appends a trace entry.
133	
134	| # | Layer | Passes when | Otherwise → outcome · reason code |

139	| 4 | **D3 WORTH IT** | `opened`: band ≥ `relevance_floor`. `escalated`: band ≥ last notified band + 1. `cleared`: the episode was notified **and** (lasted ≥ 12 h **or** peaked at USG+ above its typical band) | `suppressed` · `BELOW_RELEVANCE` / `DEDUP_SAME_BAND` / `RECOVERY_NOT_WORTH_SAYING` |
140	| 5 | **D4 PACE** | time since this episode's last notice ≥ the current gap. The gap starts at 6 h and **doubles with each notice in the same episode** (6 → 12 → 24 h), resetting when the episode closes. Severe escalations skip the wait. | `suppressed` · `COOLDOWN` |
141	| 6 | **D5 ARBITRATE** *(stub)* | the best candidate this hour for this user, by priority: escalated > opened > cleared > check-in | `suppressed` · `ARBITRATED_OUT` |
142	| 7 | **D6 RESPOND** *(stub)* | response = `notify` | — |

145	| 10 | A1 COMPOSE → A2 DELIVER *(stub)* | message composed (§9) and written to the feed | `sent` · `SENT_*` |
146	
147	### 7.3 Check-in and held notices (D8)
148	
149	- **Check-in** (`check_in.cron`, optional; clock-triggered). It evaluates the last 8 h, and speaks only if all three hold: band ≥ `relevance_floor`; `ewma ≥ 1.0` or band above `typical_band`; and no notice sent in the last 6 h. Otherwise `no_event · CHECKIN_QUIET`.
150	- **The check-in wins over quiet hours.** It's the user's explicit "talk to me now", so D8 passes it even inside the quiet window. Any notices held for that user are **absorbed** into the check-in message (`HELD_RELEASED` on each), and the check-in still counts toward the budget.
151	- **Release at quiet-hours end.** If anything is still held, all of it collapses into **one** notice about the current state. That notice goes back through D3–D7 at release time. If the episode closed overnight without ever being notified, nothing is sent (`HELD_EXPIRED`).
152	
153	---
154	
155	## 8. User rule format
156	
157	Declarative JSON in `user_rules.rules`, versioned, with `source` = `default | user | learned`. Every field is optional, and missing fields fall back to defaults.
158	
159	```json
160	{
161	  "location":        { "station_id": 4588 },
162	  "pollutants":      ["pm25"],
163	  "sensitivity":     "high",
164	  "relevance_floor": "moderate",
165	  "alert_band":      "unhealthy",
166	  "quiet_hours":     { "start": "22:00", "end": "07:00", "breakthrough_band": "very_unhealthy" },
167	  "check_in":        { "cron": "30 6 * * *" },
168	  "pace":            { "base_gap_hours": 6 },
169	  "budget":          { "max_per_day": 3 }
170	}
171	```
172	
173	| Field | Default | Layer |
174	|---|---|---|
175	| `location` | required in v1 (one station) | S3 (stub) |
176	| `sensitivity` | `default` (k = 1.0); `low` 1.25, `high` 0.75 | D1 |
177	| `relevance_floor` | `moderate` | D2, D3 |
178	| `alert_band` | `very_unhealthy`; `unhealthy` for `sensitivity: high` | D1 floor |
179	| `quiet_hours` | `22:00–07:00`, breakthrough at `very_unhealthy`; station local time | D8 |
180	| `check_in.cron` | none; 5-field cron in station local time, parsed by APScheduler's `CronTrigger.from_crontab` (live and replay) | D8 |
181	| `pace.base_gap_hours` | 6, doubling within an episode | D4 |
182	| `budget.max_per_day` | 3 non-severe | D7 |
183	
184	Validation: unknown fields are rejected, bands must be valid EPA band names, and the cron must parse. Invalid rules fall back to the previous version with `RULES_INVALID`.
185	
186	**Extension path (not v1).** New rule inputs, such as movement or home-system state, become new typed fields read by D1 or D8. Free-form conditions, if ever needed, use an `extra_conditions` block in the `business-rules` `all/any` JSON shape, evaluated by the `rule-engine` package (S-B §3). L2 ADAPT writes a new version with `source: learned`.
187	
188	---
189	
190	## 9. A1 COMPOSE contract (FR-MSG)
191	
192	The pipeline hands A1 a **structured insight**, never raw data:
193	
194	```json
195	{
196	  "kind": "opened | escalated | cleared | check_in | released_after_quiet_hours",
197	  "event_kind": "spike | climb | elevated | floor",
198	  "city": "Delhi", "local_time": "2026-10-18T08:00+05:30",
199	  "now": { "pm25": 142, "band": "very_unhealthy", "aqi": 203 },
200	  "typical_for_this_hour": { "pm25": 48, "band": "usg" },
201	  "episode": { "started": "since 2am", "hours": 6, "peak": { "pm25": 151, "at": "6am" } },
202	  "absorbed_held": [ { "kind": "opened", "at": "01:00" } ],
203	  "history_facts": ["worst since 13 Oct", "third bad morning this week"],
204	  "trend": { "direction": "rising", "per_hour": 9.5 },
205	  "user": { "name": "Arjun", "persona": { "habits": ["morning run 06:30"], "conditions": [] } },
206	  "action_candidates": ["skip the outdoor run", "keep windows closed", "wear an N95 if you go out"]
207	}
208	```
209	
210	- **History facts** are computed deterministically: "worst since `<date>`", "Nth bad day this week", "back to normal after N hours/days", "first time this month". At least one is required for spike, climb, elevated and cleared notices.
211	- **Wording by event kind:** spike → "jumped sharply"; climb → "getting worse since …"; elevated → "stuck above normal for …"; floor → "has crossed into …".
212	- **One next action** comes from a fixed catalogue keyed by `(kind, band, persona habits, local time of day)`.
213	- **Generator:** an LLM writes the sentence from this JSON. The output is validated: ≤ 220 characters, mentions exactly one action from the candidates, cites only numbers and dates present in the input. On failure or without an API key, a **template fallback** composes from the same facts. `notifications.generator` records which one ran.
214	
215	---
216	
217	## 10. RECORD vocabulary (FR-OBS)
218	
219	`outcome` ∈ `sent | held | suppressed | no_event`. `trigger` ∈ `data | clock`.
220	
221	Reason codes by layer:

334	## 8. Act: saying it well
335	
336	**A1 COMPOSE.** The decision layers hand over **verified facts**, never raw data:
337	
338	```
339	  { kind: "got worse",  city: "Delhi",  local time: 08:00,
340	    now: 142 µg/m³, Very Unhealthy,      usual for 8am: 48, USG,
341	    story: since 2am, 6 hours, peak 151 at 6am,
342	    history: "worst since 13 Oct", "third bad morning this week",
343	    person: Arjun, runs at 06:30,
344	    action options: skip the outdoor run | keep windows closed | wear an N95 outside }
345	```
346	
347	- An LLM writes one or two sentences from these facts. A validator then checks the result: short enough for a phone notification, includes exactly one of the offered actions, and cites no number or date that isn't in the facts.
348	- If the LLM fails the check or isn't available, a template writes the message from the same facts.
349	- Past context is always included for climb, spike and clearing messages ("since 2am", "worst since Tuesday", "back to normal after two rough days"). It's never a bare status like "AQI is now 142".
350	
351	**A2 DELIVER.** In the demo, a message is "delivered" when it appears in the person's feed and in the exported history. Real channels come at full scope.
352	
353	---
354	
355	## 9. Learn, and what runs across everything
356	
357	- **L1 FEEDBACK.** A person can mark a message as acted on, dismissed or not useful. In the demo, this is stored and shown next to the decision, and changes nothing.
358	- **L2 ADAPT.** Settings are stored as numbered versions, and every decision records which version it used. A future learning layer will propose a new "learned" version, never edit silently, so every change is visible and reversible.
359	- **RECORD.** Every person gets a decision row for every hour, with an outcome (sent, held, suppressed or no event), a reason code and a stage-by-stage trace of the inputs, values and results. "Why didn't I hear about it at 2am?" always has an answer, as complete as "why did I hear about it?"
360	- **REPLAY.** Nothing in the pipeline reads the real clock, and every hour is recomputed from the readings known at that moment. So replaying the past gives exactly the decisions the live system would have made. Replay is how the rules were tuned, and how caught versus missed moments are measured.
361	- **GUARD.** Not in the demo. At full scope it stands in front of every irreversible action: consent, confirmation and rate limits.
362	- **OPERATE.** Every ingestion run is logged with its freshness, failures and remaining rate limit, so the pipeline's own health is visible.
363	
364	---
365	
366	## 10. A night in Delhi, hour by hour (illustrative)
367	
368	The numbers are made up but follow the rules above. Arjun lives in Delhi and runs at 06:30. He has default sensitivity, quiet hours 22:00–07:00, and a check-in at 06:30.
369	
370	```
371	 local  band (NowCast)   station layer               Arjun's decision                         outcome
372	 -----  ---------------  --------------------------  ---------------------------------------  -------------------

374	 23:00  USG              rising                      climb needs 3 hours above the bar        no event
375	 00:00  USG              rising                      not yet                                  no event
376	 01:00  Unhealthy        CLIMB                       episode OPENS; worth it; pace, budget    held
377	                                                     ok; but quiet hours                      QUIET_HOURS_HELD
378	 02:00  Unhealthy        still climbing              same story, same band                    suppressed
379	                                                                                              DEDUP_SAME_BAND
380	 03:00  Unhealthy (peak) flat                        same story                               suppressed
381	 04:00  Unhealthy        easing                      same story                               suppressed
382	 06:30  Unhealthy        well above a usual morning  CHECK-IN wins over quiet hours; worse    SENT (one message)
383	                                                     than usual; the held message merges in
384	          "Air got worse overnight from about 1am and is still unhealthy, well above a normal
385	           Delhi morning. Maybe skip the outdoor run today and try an indoor workout."
386	 07:00  Unhealthy        -                           quiet hours end; nothing left to release  -
387	 10:00  Unhealthy        -                           same story, same band                     suppressed
388	 14:00  USG              calm hour 1                 episode RECOVERING                        no event
389	 17:00  USG              calm hour 4                 episode CLOSES; it lasted 16h, so worth   SENT
390	                                                     saying; 10.5h since last, pace ok
391	          "Delhi's air is back to its usual level after a rough 16 hours. If you missed your
392	           run this morning, the evening looks fine for it."
393	```
394	
395	Two messages in about 20 hours, each with context and one action. Every silent hour has a logged reason.
396

398

"""The only module allowed to read wall-clock time. Everything else receives a Clock."""
from __future__ import annotations

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from typing import Protocol


class Clock(Protocol):
    def now(self) -> datetime: ...


class SystemClock:
    def now(self) -> datetime:
        return datetime.now(timezone.utc)


class FixedClock:
    def __init__(self, t: datetime):
        if t.tzinfo is None:
            raise ValueError("FixedClock needs a timezone-aware datetime")
        self._t = t

    def now(self) -> datetime:
        return self._t

    def set(self, t: datetime) -> None:
        self._t = t

    def advance(self, delta: timedelta) -> None:
        self._t = self._t + delta

# Building LLM-Powered Applications with Claude

This skill helps you build LLM-powered applications with Claude. Choose the right surface based on your needs, detect the project language, then read the relevant language-specific documentation.

## Before You Start

Scan the target file (or, if no target file, the prompt and project) for non-Anthropic provider markers - `import openai`, `from openai`, `langchain_openai`, `OpenAI(`, `gpt-4`, `gpt-5`, file names like `agent-openai.py` or `*-generic.py`, or any explicit instruction to keep the code provider-neutral. If you find any, stop and tell the user that this skill produces Claude/Anthropic SDK code; ask whether they want to switch the file to Claude or want a non-Claude implementation. Do not edit a non-Anthropic file with Anthropic SDK calls. (Exception: the `prompt-audit` subcommand is non-interactive and does not stop here - it records non-Anthropic provider markers in its report's stated assumptions and never proposes switching a non-Anthropic file to the Anthropic SDK.)

## Output Requirement

When the user asks you to add, modify, or implement a Claude feature, your code must call Claude through one of:

1. **The official Anthropic SDK** for the project's language (`anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, `com.anthropic.*`, etc.). This is the default whenever a supported SDK exists for the project.
2. **Raw HTTP** (`curl`, `requests`, `fetch`, `httpx`, etc.) - only when the user explicitly asks for cURL/REST/raw HTTP, the project is a shell/cURL project, or the language has no official SDK.

Never mix the two - don't reach for `requests`/`fetch` in a Python or TypeScript project just because it feels lighter. Never fall back to OpenAI-compatible shims.

**Never guess SDK usage.** Function names, class names, namespaces, method signatures, and import paths must come from explicit documentation - either the `{lang}/` files in this skill or the official SDK repositories or documentation links listed in `shared/live-sources.md`. If the binding you need is not explicitly documented in the skill files, WebFetch the relevant SDK repo from `shared/live-sources.md` before writing code. Do not infer Ruby/Java/Go/PHP/C# APIs from cURL shapes or from another language's SDK.

**If WebFetch or repository access fails** (network restricted, timeouts, clone blocked): do not keep retrying - write code from the patterns and namespace/package tables in the `{lang}/` file, run the compiler or interpreter on it, and iterate on the error output. For statically-typed SDKs (C#, Java, Go) a compile-fix loop against local errors reaches working code faster than blocked network research.

## Defaults

Unless the user requests otherwise:

For the Claude model version, please use Claude Opus 5.5, which you can access via the exact model string `claude-opus-5-5`. Please default to using adaptive thinking (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`) for anything remotely complicated. And finally, please default to streaming for any request that may involve long input, long output, or high `max_tokens` - it prevents hitting request timeouts. Use the SDK's `.get_final_message()` / `.finalMessage()` helper to get the complete response if you don't need to handle individual stream events. When a streaming request defines user-defined (client) tools, set `eager_input_streaming: true` on each of those tools so large tool inputs (file contents, code, documents) stream as they are generated instead of arriving in one burst after the server finishes buffering them; the client then owns validation: the SDKs' tolerant parsers can return a silently truncated input instead of raising, so validate each parsed tool input against its schema before running it (the typed runner helpers such as `betaZodTool` / typed `@beta_tool` do this; `betaTool()` JSON-Schema tools and manual loops must validate themselves), treat a failure like invalid JSON (`INVALID_JSON` error `tool_result` when you hold the block, re-issue otherwise), check `max_tokens` / `refusal` stop reasons before running tools, and catch only the SDK's JSON error, never its typed API errors - pattern in `shared/tool-use-concepts.md` -> Eager input streaming. Leave it off for non-streaming requests, for server tools, and when the request goes through a proxy or an older Bedrock model deployment that rejects the field.

## Warning: API Drift - Your Training Prior May Be Stale

Several common Claude API shapes changed in 2025-2026. If you recall a pattern from training, verify it against the `{lang}/` files in this skill before writing - the rows below are the most frequent drift points:

## Which Surface Should I Use?

> **Start simple.** Default to the simplest tier that meets your needs. Single API calls and workflows handle most use cases - only reach for agents when the task genuinely requires open-ended, model-driven exploration. "Simplest" means the least code you own: for a hosted, scheduled, or memory-backed agent, Managed Agents is usually the simplest option (no loop code, no state files, no scheduler), even though it's a bigger platform.

| Use Case                                        | Tier            | Recommended Surface       | Why                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Classification, summarization, extraction, Q&A  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | One request, one response                                    |
| Batch processing or embeddings                  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | Specialized endpoints                                        |
| Multi-step pipelines with code-controlled logic | Workflow        | **Claude API + tool use** | You orchestrate the loop                                     |
| Custom agent with your own tools                | Agent           | **Claude API + tool use** | Maximum flexibility                                          |
| Server-managed stateful agent with workspace    | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Anthropic runs the loop and hosts the tool-execution sandbox |
| Persisted, versioned agent configs              | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Agents are stored objects; sessions pin to a version         |
| Long-running multi-turn agent with file mounts  | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Per-session containers, SSE event stream, Skills + MCP       |
| Agent that runs on a schedule (cron, "every night") | Agent       | **Managed Agents** - scheduled deployments | Deployments fire sessions autonomously; no client-side scheduler |
| One deliverable that must meet a quality bar ("until it's right") | Agent | **Managed Agents** - outcomes | A separate grader iterates the agent against your rubric until it passes |
| Agent work too big to hand out one task at a time | Agent | **Managed Agents** - dynamic workflows | Many agents in phases |

> **Note:** Managed Agents is the right choice when you want Anthropic to run the agent loop *and* host the container where tools execute - file ops, bash, code execution all run in the per-session workspace. If you want to host the compute yourself or run your own custom tool runtime, Claude API + tool use is the right choice - use the tool runner for the agentic loop - its per-turn hooks still give you approval gates, logging, error interception, and conditional execution (see `shared/tool-use-concepts.md`) - or the manual loop when you want to own the entire loop yourself.

> **Cloud-provider access.** **Claude Platform on AWS** is Anthropic-operated with same-day API parity - see `shared/claude-platform-on-aws.md` for client setup. For per-feature availability on **Claude Platform on AWS**, **Amazon Bedrock**, **Google Vertex AI**, and **Microsoft Foundry**, see `shared/platform-availability.md` - that table is the single source of truth in this skill; do not infer availability from anywhere else.

### Building an Agent: Four Approaches

Once you've decided you actually need an agent (open-ended, model-driven tool use), there are four distinct ways to build one. Two independent questions separate them: **who supplies the harness** (the agent loop + context management) and **who supplies the deployment** (the infra the agent runs on). The Tool Runner and the Claude Agent SDK both supply a *harness only* - you still host and deploy them yourself - which is why they're easy to conflate. Managed Agents (CMA) is the only option that supplies **both** the harness *and* managed deployment; the manual loop supplies neither.

| # | Approach | You write | Harness & deployment | Tools available | Use when |
|---|----------|-----------|----------------------|-----------------|----------|
| 1 | **Claude API - manual loop** | The `while stop_reason == "tool_use"` loop yourself | You build the harness; you host | Only tools you define | You want to own the *entire* loop - no beta dependency, or a control flow the Tool Runner's per-turn hooks don't fit |
| 2 | **Claude API - Tool Runner** (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner` + `@beta_tool` / `betaZodTool`) | Just the tool functions | SDK supplies the loop (**harness only**); you host | Only tools you define | A custom-tool agent without hand-writing the loop (most cases). Per-turn hooks still give you approval gates, error interception, result modification (e.g. `cache_control`), retries, streaming, and compaction |
| 3 | **Managed Agents** (REST, beta) | Agent config + your tool results | Anthropic supplies the harness **and** hosts a per-session sandbox (**harness + deployment**) | Anthropic-hosted sandbox (bash, files, code exec) + Skills/MCP + your tools | You want Anthropic to run the loop *and* host the per-session workspace; persisted/versioned configs; long-running sessions |
| 4 | **Claude Agent SDK** - *separate product* (`claude-agent-sdk` / `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) | A prompt + options | SDK supplies the Claude Code harness + built-in tools (**harness only**); you host | Built-in Read/Write/Edit/Bash/Glob/Grep/WebSearch/WebFetch + MCP + subagents | You want a batteries-included coding/filesystem agent running on your own infra |

The harness/deployment split is the key mental model: options 1, 2, and 4 all **leave deployment to you**; only option 3 (CMA) adds managed deployment. Options 1-3 are what this skill generates; option 4 is a different library with its own docs - see the disambiguation below.

> **Tool Runner != Claude Agent SDK.** These sound alike but are different packages:
> - **Tool Runner** is part of the regular Anthropic API SDK (`anthropic` / `@anthropic-ai/sdk`), reached via `client.beta.messages.tool_runner`. It automates the request -> execute -> loop cycle *for tools you define*. No built-in tools, no filesystem access, no sandbox - you supply every tool and host the compute. It is option 2 above, a thin helper over `POST /v1/messages`.
> - **Claude Agent SDK** (`claude-agent-sdk` / `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) is Claude Code packaged as a library. It ships built-in tools (file read/write/edit, bash, grep, web search), the full agent loop, context management, hooks, subagents, permissions, and sessions. You call `query(prompt, options)` and it drives everything.
>
> Both are **harness-only - you host and deploy them.** The difference is scope of harness: the Tool Runner loops over tools *you* define (with per-turn hooks for approval, interception, result modification, and retries - but no built-in tools); the Agent SDK is the full Claude Code harness with built-in tools. Neither provides managed deployment - that's what **Managed Agents (CMA)** adds (Anthropic hosts the loop and a per-session sandbox).
>
> **This skill covers the Claude API and Managed Agents (options 1-3); it does not generate Claude Agent SDK code.** If the user actually wants the Claude Agent SDK, point them to its docs (`code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk`) - don't substitute the API Tool Runner for it, or vice-versa.

### Should I Build an Agent?

Before choosing the agent tier, check all four criteria:

- **Complexity** - Is the task multi-step and hard to fully specify in advance? (e.g., "turn this design doc into a PR" vs. "extract the title from this PDF")
- **Value** - Does the outcome justify higher cost and latency?
- **Viability** - Is Claude capable at this task type?
- **Cost of error** - Can errors be caught and recovered from? (tests, review, rollback)

If the answer is "no" to any of these, stay at a simpler tier (single call or workflow).

## Architecture

Everything goes through `POST /v1/messages`. Tools and output constraints are features of this single endpoint - not separate APIs.

**User-defined tools** - You define tools (via decorators, Zod schemas, or raw JSON), and the SDK's tool runner handles calling the API, executing your functions, and looping until Claude is done. For full control, you can write the loop manually.

**Server-side tools** - Anthropic-hosted tools that run on Anthropic's infrastructure. Code execution is fully server-side (declare it in `tools`, Claude runs code automatically). Computer use can be server-hosted or self-hosted.

**Structured outputs** - Constrains the Messages API response format (`output_config.format`) and/or tool parameter validation (`strict: true`). The recommended approach is `client.messages.parse()` which validates responses against your schema automatically. Note: the old `output_format` parameter is deprecated; use `output_config: {format: {...}}` on `messages.create()`.

**Supporting endpoints** - Batches (`POST /v1/messages/batches`), Files (`POST /v1/files`), Token Counting (`POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` - see `shared/token-counting.md`), and Models (`GET /v1/models`, `GET /v1/models/{id}` - live capability/context-window discovery) feed into or support Messages API requests.
